Expectation1: Communicate any challenges or concerns promptly to the mentor.
Situation1: A serious conflict with teammates is threatening the mentee’s deliverable timeline.
Expectation2: Challenge unfair systems and influence policy change
Situation2: They gather recurring cases of unfair treatment and bring them to discussions with community leaders or officials.
Story: I sat at my desk, staring at the email draft to my mentor. As a mentee, I was expected to communicate any challenges promptly, and the conflict with my teammates was spiraling out of control. Our project deadline was at risk, and I knew my mentor would want to know immediately. But as an advocate, I had just collected several stories of unfair treatment from my peers—stories that mirrored my own situation. I was supposed to bring these cases to the community leaders tomorrow, challenging the very system that my mentor was a part of. If I reached out to my mentor now, would I be betraying the trust of those who confided in me? Would I be seen as just another complainer, undermining my credibility as an advocate? My hands hovered over the keyboard, torn between the responsibility to be transparent with my mentor and the duty to protect and represent my peers. The weight of both roles pressed down on me, and I felt paralyzed, caught between conflicting expectations and unsure which path to take.
